newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council expected to back new Haiti operation.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council expected to back new Haiti operation.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council gave its general support to keeping U.N. troops in Haiti an extra four months during consultations on Friday, council president Peter Osvald of Sweden said.

Support of Secretary-General Kofi Annan's call for a continued U.N. presence seemed to dispel fears that China and Russia might try to block a follow-on operation in Haiti when the current U.N. force's mandate expires on July 31.
"There was general support for the recommendations contained in the secretary-general's report concerning a continued international presence in Haiti until November of this year," Osvald said.
"Work has started on a draft resolution which will, in all likelihood, be adopted by the middle of next week."
The last renewal of the current U.N. force, called the U.N. Support Mission in Haiti (UNSMIH), was billed as its final extension, with China and Russia particularly opposed to any further renewal.

China has been irked in the past by Haiti's links with Taiwan, which Beijing considers a renegade province. Russia contrasts the Haiti operation with the small U.N. observer mission in the former Soviet republic of Georgia, where a Russian-led force is monitoring a ceasefire between government troops and Abkhazian secessionists.

But Annan, citing the "daunting political and economic challenges" still facing the impoverished Caribbean nation, recommended setting up a new operation, to be called the U.N. Transition Mission in Haiti (UNTMIH).
It would have a four-month mandate, with 250 police instead of the present 300, and a headquarters staff of only 50 troops, compared to the 500 now in Haiti.

Annan also recommended supplementary troop contingents to be provided by Canada and Pakistan and funded by voluntary contributions from Canada and the United States. He did not give the size of the proposed contingents.

In addition to the 500 U.N. troops currently in Haiti, 800 more Canadian and Pakistani soldiers are part of the operation but are paid for by the United States and Canada, to meet Chinese and Russian objections to a more costly force.
